syros.name: Syros
syros.summary: A Greek island in the Cyclades whose capital, Ermoupoli, was a more important port than Piraeus during the 19th century.

melce-t-tabb-h-n.name: Melceü't-Tabbâhîn
melce-t-tabb-h-n.summary: The first Ottoman Turkish cookbook, written in 1844 by Hoca Mehmed Kâmil, later translated into English and Arabic.

tyrnavos.name: Tyrnavos
tyrnavos.summary: Town and municipality in the Larissa regional unit of Thessaly, Greece, with about 11,000 residents in the town itself. It is the second-largest town in its regional unit.

tsipouro.name: Tsipouro
tsipouro.summary: Un-aged Greek brandy of 40–45% alcohol, made from grape pomace or directly from wine. It is typically double-distilled and sometimes flavored with anise.

arak-drink.name: Arak
arak-drink.summary: Distilled spirit from the Levant, part of the anise drinks family.

grappa.name: Grappa
grappa.summary: Italian brandy of 35 to 60 percent alcohol, distilled from the grape skins, seeds and stems left over from winemaking. It is usually served after dinner to aid digestion.

thessaly.name: Thessaly
thessaly.summary: A geographic and administrative region of northern central Greece, formerly known as Aeolia, which became part of the modern Greek state in 1881.

meyhane.name: Meyhane
meyhane.summary: Traditional restaurant or bar in Turkey, the Balkans, Azerbaijan and Iran, serving alcoholic drinks such as wine, rakı or beer with meze and traditional foods.

meze.name: meze
meze.summary: A selection of small appetizer dishes served in Eastern Mediterranean cuisines, similar to Spanish tapas, often accompanied by spirits such as ouzo or raki.

ouzo-plomari.name: Ouzo Plomari
ouzo-plomari.summary: Historic Greek ouzo company on the island of Lesvos, founded in 1894 by Plomari native Isidoros Arvanitis. It now exports to more than 40 countries.

plomari.name: Plomari
plomari.summary: Town on the Greek island of Lesbos, the second largest on the island and its only sizable coastal settlement in the south. It had a 2021 census population of 4,852 for its municipal unit.

spasenija-pata-markovi.name: Spasenija Pata Marković
spasenija-pata-markovi.summary: Serbian cookbook author (1881–1974) whose My Cookbook, published in 1939, became known as Pata's Cookbook. It is considered the most extensive collection of recipes written in Serbia.

kalamata.name: Kalamata
kalamata.summary: Second most populous city of the Peloponnese in southern Greece, and capital and chief port of Messenia. It is famed for its olives, olive oil and the Kalamatianos dance.

biedermeier.name: Biedermeier
biedermeier.summary: An era in the art and culture of the German Confederation from 1815 to 1848, when the growing middle classes shaped unchallenging, appealing styles in literature, music and design.

theophil-hansen.name: Theophil Hansen
theophil-hansen.summary: A Danish architect (1813–1891) who became an Austrian citizen and was known for Neoclassical buildings in Athens and Vienna.

ernst-ziller.name: Ernst Ziller
ernst-ziller.summary: German-born architect (1837–1923) who became a Greek citizen and designed many royal and municipal buildings in Athens and other Greek cities.

stamatios-kleanthis.name: Stamatios Kleanthis
stamatios-kleanthis.summary: Greek architect who lived from 1802 to 1862.

theodoros-vryzakis.name: Theodoros Vryzakis
theodoros-vryzakis.summary: Greek painter (1814–1878) known for historical scenes and a founder of the Munich School of Greek artists.

dionysios-tsokos.name: Dionysios Tsokos
dionysios-tsokos.summary: Greek painter (c. 1814/1820–1862), one of the first to gain recognition in post-Ottoman Greece, known for portraits and historical scenes.

nikiforos-lytras.name: Nikiforos Lytras
nikiforos-lytras.summary: Greek painter (1832–1904) trained in Munich who became a professor at the Athens School of Arts, known for ethnographic scenes and portraits, including of King Otto and Queen Amalia.

georgios-jakobides.name: Georgios Jakobides
georgios-jakobides.summary: Greek painter and medallist (1853-1932), a leading figure of the Munich School, who founded and was first curator of the National Gallery of Greece.

nemanji-dynasty.name: Nemanjić dynasty
nemanji-dynasty.summary: Serbia's most prominent medieval royal house, producing twelve monarchs from 1166 to 1371 and overseeing the kingdom's rise to an empire under Stefan Dušan.

ura-jak-i.name: Đura Jakšić
ura-jak-i.summary: A Serbian poet, painter, writer and dramatist, 1832 to 1878.

pavle-simi.name: Pavle Simić
pavle-simi.summary: A Serbian Romantic-era painter, 1818 to 1876, from Novi Sad, considered one of the most significant artists of his time.

konstantinos-volanakis.name: Konstantinos Volanakis
konstantinos-volanakis.summary: Greek painter (c. 1837–1907) known as one of the greatest Greek seascape painters.

ioannis-altamouras.name: Ioannis Altamouras
ioannis-altamouras.summary: Greek painter (1852–1878) known for his seascapes, a contemporary of fellow marine painter Konstantinos Volanakis.

nikolaos-gyzis.name: Nikolaos Gyzis
nikolaos-gyzis.summary: Greek painter (1842–1901) and leading figure of the Munich School, best known for his painting "Eros and the Painter."

athens-school-of-fine-arts.name: Athens School of Fine Arts
athens-school-of-fine-arts.summary: Greek higher education institution based in Athens that specializes in the visual arts.

georgios-roilos.name: Georgios Roilos
georgios-roilos.summary: Greek painter (1867-1928) of the Munich School known for historical scenes and portraits, including 'The Poets', depicting the Generation of 1880 poets.

p-ricl-s-pantazis.name: Périclès Pantazis
p-ricl-s-pantazis.summary: Greek impressionist painter (1849–1884) who built much of his artistic reputation in Belgium during the 19th century.

eleftherios-venizelos.name: Eleftherios Venizelos
eleftherios-venizelos.summary: Greek statesman who served as prime minister for over 12 years between 1910 and 1933, leading reforms and helping Greece expand after the Balkan Wars.

constantine-i-of-greece.name: Constantine I of Greece
constantine-i-of-greece.summary: King of Greece (1913–1917, 1920–1922) whose pro-German stance during World War I caused the National Schism, splitting the country.

filiki-eteria.name: Filiki Eteria
filiki-eteria.summary: A secret revolutionary society founded in Odessa in 1814 to overthrow Ottoman rule in Greece, which launched the Greek War of Independence in 1821.

nikolaos-skoufas.name: Nikolaos Skoufas
nikolaos-skoufas.summary: Founding member of the Filiki Eteria, a Greek conspiratorial organization against the Ottoman Empire that prepared the Greek War of Independence; he lived from 1779 to 1818.

emmanuil-xanthos.name: Emmanuil Xanthos
emmanuil-xanthos.summary: Greek merchant (1772–1852) and one of the founders of the Filiki Eteria, a secret society that opposed the Ottoman Empire.

athanasios-tsakalov.name: Athanasios Tsakalov
athanasios-tsakalov.summary: Greek patriot (1790 to 1851) and member of the Filiki Eteria, a secret society working toward Greek liberation from Ottoman rule.

battle-of-navarino.name: Battle of Navarino
battle-of-navarino.summary: A naval battle on 20 October 1827 in Navarino Bay, Greece, where British, French and Russian forces destroyed an Ottoman-Egyptian fleet, making Greek independence more likely; the last major sea battle fought entirely by sailing ships.

greco-turkish-war-1897.name: Greco-Turkish War of 1897
greco-turkish-war-1897.summary: A brief 1897 war between Greece and the Ottoman Empire over the status of Crete; despite Ottoman victory on the battlefield, Crete gained autonomy the following year.

goudi-coup.name: Goudi coup
goudi-coup.summary: A 1909 military coup near Athens that ended Greece's old political system, eventually bringing Eleftherios Venizelos to power and ushering in sweeping reforms.

hydra-class-ironclad.name: Hydra class
hydra-class-ironclad.summary: A class of three Greek ironclad warships built in the 1880s and 1890s, obsolete and too slow by the time of the First Balkan War.

jakov-nenadovi.name: Jakov Nenadović
jakov-nenadovi.summary: Serbian voivode and politician (1765–1836) who served as Serbia's first prime minister and interior minister, a leading figure alongside Karađorđe.

valjevo.name: Valjevo
valjevo.summary: A city in western Serbia on the Kolubara River, the administrative center of the Kolubara District, with over 56,000 residents as of 2022.

first-serbian-uprising.name: First Serbian Uprising
first-serbian-uprising.summary: An uprising of Serbs against Ottoman rule from 1804 to 1813, starting as a revolt against renegade Janissary officers and growing into the Serbian Revolution.

treaty-of-adrianople-1829.name: Treaty of Adrianople
treaty-of-adrianople-1829.summary: Ended the Russo-Turkish War of 1828–29, giving Russia new Black Sea territory and access to the Danube mouths, and opening the Dardanelles to all commercial ships.

mihail-savov.name: Mihail Savov
mihail-savov.summary: A Bulgarian general (1857–1928) who served as assistant commander-in-chief of the army during the Balkan Wars and twice as Minister of War.

ferdinand-i-of-bulgaria.name: Ferdinand I of Bulgaria
ferdinand-i-of-bulgaria.summary: Monarch of Bulgaria from 1887 to 1918, ruling first as Prince then as Tsar; under him Bulgaria gained independence from the Ottoman Empire and fought in the Balkan Wars and World War I before he abdicated.

bregalnica.name: Bregalnica
bregalnica.summary: The second-largest river in North Macedonia, flowing from near Pehchevo to join the Vardar, and site of the Battle of Bregalnica.

nigrita.name: Nigrita
nigrita.summary: A city in the Serres regional unit of Macedonia, Greece, south of the Strymonas river, about 22 km south of Serres and 92 km northeast of Thessaloniki.

emmanouil-tombazis.name: Emmanouil Tombazis
emmanouil-tombazis.summary: Greek naval captain from Hydra (c. 1784–1831) active in the Greek War of Independence, who served as Commissioner of Crete in 1823–1824 and briefly as naval minister in 1828.

gergeri.name: Gergeri
gergeri.summary: A village on Crete, seat of Rouvas municipal unit, where in 1823 Emmanouil Tombazis gathered 3,000 Cretans to face a much larger Turkish-Egyptian force.

vuk-karad-i.name: Vuk Karadžić
vuk-karad-i.summary: Serbian philologist and linguist (1787-1864) who reformed the modern Serbian language, compiled folk tales, wrote the first Serbian dictionary, and translated the New Testament.

dionysios-solomos.name: Dionysios Solomos
dionysios-solomos.summary: Greek poet (1798–1857) from Zakynthos considered Greece's national poet, best known for writing the Hymn to Liberty, which became the Greek national anthem in 1865.

aristotelis-valaoritis.name: Aristotelis Valaoritis
aristotelis-valaoritis.summary: Greek poet and politician (1824–1879), a leading figure of the Heptanese School regarded as a national poet for his verse on the Greek War of Independence.

alexandros-rizos-rangavis.name: Alexandros Rizos Rangavis
alexandros-rizos-rangavis.summary: A 19th-century Greek man of letters, poet and statesman (1809–1892).

panagiotis-soutsos.name: Panagiotis Soutsos
panagiotis-soutsos.summary: Greek poet, novelist and journalist (1806-1868) born in Constantinople, a pioneer of Greek romanticism who helped inspire the revival of the modern Olympic Games.

national-theatre-of-greece.name: National Theatre of Greece
national-theatre-of-greece.summary: Greece's national theatre, based in Athens.

gregorios-xenopoulos.name: Gregorios Xenopoulos
gregorios-xenopoulos.summary: A Greek novelist, journalist and playwright from Zakynthos (1867 to 1951) who edited the magazine The Education of Children for decades and founded Nea Estia and the Society of Greek Writers.

theodoros-kolokotronis.name: Theodoros Kolokotronis
theodoros-kolokotronis.summary: Greek general (1770–1843) and leading commander of the Greek War of Independence, celebrated for his 1822 victory at the Battle of Dervenakia.

yannis-makriyannis.name: Yannis Makriyannis
yannis-makriyannis.summary: Greek general and self-taught author (1797–1864) whose Memoirs, written in vernacular Demotic Greek, became a landmark of modern Greek literature.

emmanuel-rhoides.name: Emmanuel Rhoides
emmanuel-rhoides.summary: Greek writer, journalist and translator (1836–1904), one of the most influential 19th-century Greek authors, best known internationally for his novel The Papess Joanne.

demetrios-vikelas.name: Demetrios Vikelas
demetrios-vikelas.summary: A Greek businessman and writer (1835-1908) who co-founded the International Olympic Committee and served as its first president from 1894 to 1896.

johann-georg-von-hahn.name: Johann Georg von Hahn
johann-georg-von-hahn.summary: German diplomat and philologist (1811–1869) who served as Austrian consul in Ioannina and later Athens, and is considered the founder of Albanian studies.

first-athenian-school.name: First Athenian School
first-athenian-school.summary: Romantic literary movement in Athens between 1830 and 1880, following Greek independence, whose leading members were largely of Phanariote origin.

holger-pedersen-linguist.name: Holger Pedersen
holger-pedersen-linguist.summary: Danish linguist (1867-1953) who made major contributions to language science and wrote about thirty authoritative works on several languages.

elodie-lawton.name: Elodie Lawton
elodie-lawton.summary: A British author who lived in Boston in the 1850s and was an advocate of the abolitionist movement.

ripanj.name: Ripanj
ripanj.summary: A suburban settlement of Belgrade, Serbia, notable as the largest village in the country by both population and land area.

august-zeune.name: August Zeune
august-zeune.summary: German geographer and academic (1778–1853) who founded the Berlin Blind School and was an authority on geography and Germanic languages.

balkan-mountains.name: Balkan Mountains
balkan-mountains.summary: A roughly 560-kilometre range in Bulgaria running from the Serbian border to the Black Sea, reaching 2,376 metres at Botev Peak and forming the country's north-south divide.

carl-ritter.name: Carl Ritter
carl-ritter.summary: German geographer (1779–1859) considered, with Alexander von Humboldt, a founder of modern geography, and the first professor of geography at the University of Berlin.

hermann-wagner-geographer.name: Hermann Wagner
hermann-wagner-geographer.summary: German geographer and cartographer (1840–1929) who held geography professorships at Königsberg and Göttingen and edited major geographical journals.

marion-newbigin.name: Marion Newbigin
marion-newbigin.summary: Scottish geographer, biologist and academic author (1869–1934), noted for her book Animal Geography and for editing the Scottish Geographical Magazine.

albrecht-penck.name: Albrecht Penck
albrecht-penck.summary: German geographer and geologist (1858–1945), father of fellow geographer Walther Penck.

heinrich-kiepert.name: Heinrich Kiepert
heinrich-kiepert.summary: A German geographer who lived from 1818 to 1899.

congress-of-berlin.name: Congress of Berlin
congress-of-berlin.summary: An 1878 meeting of Europe's major powers that revised the Treaty of San Stefano and reorganized the borders of southeastern Europe after the Russo-Turkish War.

ami-bou.name: Ami Boué
ami-bou.summary: A French Huguenot geologist (1794–1881) who studied strata and fossils across Europe, opposed catastrophism, and was among the first to produce a geological map of the world.

guillaume-lejean.name: Guillaume Lejean
guillaume-lejean.summary: A French explorer and ethnographer (1828–1871) from Brittany.

treaty-of-constantinople-1832.name: Treaty of Constantinople (1832)
treaty-of-constantinople-1832.summary: Concluded in July 1832 following the London Conference, it set the new Kingdom of Greece's northern border along the Arta–Volos line.

megali-idea.name: Megali Idea
megali-idea.summary: Greek nationalist idea, first named in 1844, aiming to unite all Greek-populated lands and revive the Byzantine Empire; it shaped Greek politics until 1923.

balkan-league.name: Balkan League
balkan-league.summary: A 1912 alliance of Greece, Bulgaria, Serbia and Montenegro against the Ottoman Empire, spearheaded by Eleftherios Venizelos; its First Balkan War victory was followed by a split among the allies.

east-thrace.name: Eastern Thrace
east-thrace.summary: The part of Turkey geographically in Southeast Europe, separated from Anatolia by the Dardanelles, Sea of Marmara and Bosphorus, and including part of Istanbul.

july-crisis.name: July Crisis
july-crisis.summary: The chain of diplomatic and military escalations among European powers in mid-1914, beginning with the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, that led to the outbreak of World War I.

otto-of-greece.name: Otto of Greece
otto-of-greece.summary: Bavarian prince who became King of Greece in 1832 at age 17, ruled as an absolute monarch until granting a constitution in 1843, and was deposed in 1862.

3-september-1843-revolution.name: 3 September 1843 Revolution
3-september-1843-revolution.summary: An 1843 uprising by the Hellenic Army and Athenian citizens against King Otto's absolute rule, forcing him to grant a constitution and end Bavarian control of the government.

george-i-of-greece.name: George I of Greece
george-i-of-greece.summary: Danish-born prince elected king of Greece in 1863 at age 17, reigning almost 50 years, the longest in modern Greek history, until his assassination in 1913.

alexandros-koumoundouros.name: Alexandros Koumoundouros
alexandros-koumoundouros.summary: A Greek politician (1815–1883) who served as Prime Minister of Greece ten times between 1865 and 1882, amid a turbulent period of Greek history.

charilaos-trikoupis.name: Charilaos Trikoupis
charilaos-trikoupis.summary: Greek politician (1832-1896) who served as prime minister seven times, funded the Corinth Canal, and is considered the founder of modern Greece.

greek-constitution-of-1864.name: Greek Constitution of 1864
greek-constitution-of-1864.summary: A constitution drafted by Greece's Second National Assembly of 1863 to 1864, shifting the country from a constitutional monarchy to a crowned republic.

greek-constitution-of-1911.name: Greek Constitution of 1911
greek-constitution-of-1911.summary: A major revision of Greece's 1864 constitution, enacted after Eleftherios Venizelos rose to power following the 1909 Goudi revolt.

young-turks.name: Young Turks
young-turks.summary: A broad opposition movement against Sultan Abdul Hamid II's absolutist rule, whose Committee of Union and Progress prevailed in the 1908 revolution.

committee-of-union-and-progress.name: Committee of Union and Progress
committee-of-union-and-progress.summary: An Ottoman revolutionary group, secret society and political party active from 1889 to 1926, associated with the 'Young Turks', that forced restoration of the 1876 constitution in 1908.

abdul-hamid-ii.name: Abdul Hamid II
abdul-hamid-ii.summary: 34th sultan of the Ottoman Empire (1876–1909), the last to hold effective control over the fracturing state, who suspended the constitution in 1878 and ruled with absolute power.

mehmed-v.name: Mehmed V
mehmed-v.summary: Penultimate Ottoman sultan (r. 1909–1918), a largely powerless constitutional monarch whose reign saw the Balkan Wars and entry into World War I.

edessa-greece.name: Edessa, Greece
edessa-greece.summary: A city in Northern Greece, known until 1923 as Vodena, once a major textile-industry center and a flashpoint of Greek-Bulgarian tension in the late 19th century.

bulgarian-exarchate.name: Bulgarian Exarchate
bulgarian-exarchate.summary: Official name of the Bulgarian Orthodox Church from its establishment by Ottoman decree in 1870/1872 until 1945, declared schismatic by the Patriarchate of Constantinople and central to forming the modern Bulgarian nation.

dodecanese.name: Dodecanese
dodecanese.summary: A group of Greek islands in the southeastern Aegean Sea off the coast of Anatolia, with Rhodes as the dominant island since antiquity.

italo-turkish-war.name: Italo-Turkish War
italo-turkish-war.summary: An 1911–1912 war between the Kingdom of Italy and the Ottoman Empire, after which Italy took Libya and the Dodecanese islands; seen as a precursor to World War I.

petrovi-njego-dynasty.name: Petrović-Njegoš dynasty
petrovi-njego-dynasty.summary: A Serbian noble family that ruled Montenegro from 1697 to 1918, first as prince-bishops and then, from 1852, as a princely dynasty.

prince-bishopric-of-montenegro.name: Prince-Bishopric of Montenegro
prince-bishopric-of-montenegro.summary: A Serbian Orthodox ecclesiastical principality, 1516 to 1852, whose bishops, or prince-bishops, ruled Montenegro as a theocracy after defying Ottoman overlordship.

stefanos-dragoumis.name: Stefanos Dragoumis
stefanos-dragoumis.summary: A Greek judge, writer and Prime Minister of Greece from January to October 1910, and father of Ion Dragoumis.

macedonian-committee.name: Macedonian Committee
macedonian-committee.summary: Greek revolutionary organization aiming to liberate Macedonia from Ottoman rule, active during the early 1900s Macedonian Struggle alongside Bulgarian and Serb groups.

macedonian-struggle.name: Macedonian Struggle
macedonian-struggle.summary: Series of conflicts, mainly between Greek and Bulgarian factions, fought over Ottoman Macedonia between 1893 and 1912, largely ending with the 1908 Young Turk Revolution.

theophilos-kairis.name: Theophilos Kairis
theophilos-kairis.summary: Greek Eastern Orthodox priest, philosopher, and revolutionary (1784–1853), born in Andros to a distinguished family.

petar-ii-petrovi-njego.name: Petar II Petrović-Njegoš
petar-ii-petrovi-njego.summary: Prince-Bishop of Montenegro (1813 to 1851), also a poet and philosopher; he united Montenegro's tribes, introduced taxation and law reforms, and fought the Ottoman Empire throughout his rule.

adamantios-korais.name: Adamantios Korais
adamantios-korais.summary: Greek scholar (1748–1833) credited with laying the foundations of modern Greek literature and a major figure of the Greek Enlightenment, whose work helped pave the way for the Greek War of Independence.

modern-greek-enlightenment.name: Modern Greek Enlightenment
modern-greek-enlightenment.summary: The Greek expression of the Age of Enlightenment, an intellectual movement among Greeks then scattered across the Ottoman Empire, the Ionian Islands, Venice and Italy, which served as its educational center.

hellenic-nomarchy.name: Hellenic Nomarchy
hellenic-nomarchy.summary: An anonymous 1806 pamphlet published in Italy advocating freedom, social justice and equality, considered a key text of Greek republicanism read widely before the 1821 War of Independence.

konstantinos-koumas.name: Konstantinos Koumas
konstantinos-koumas.summary: Greek 'Teacher of the Nation' (1777–1836), a pioneer of the Modern Greek Enlightenment who worked as a historian, philosopher and translator.

neophytos-vamvas.name: Neophytos Vamvas
neophytos-vamvas.summary: A Greek priest, philosopher and educator (1770–1856) who became the first dean of philosophy at the University of Athens and translated the Bible into modern Greek, sparking controversy.

homer.name: Homer
homer.summary: Ancient Greek poet, possibly born around the 8th century BC, traditionally credited as author of the Iliad and the Odyssey, foundational works of Greek literature.

skiathos.name: Skiathos
skiathos.summary: A small Greek island in the northwest Aegean Sea, part of the Northern Sporades archipelago.

ecumenical-patriarchate-of-constantinopl.name: Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople
ecumenical-patriarchate-of-constantinopl.summary: One of the autocephalous churches of Eastern Orthodox Christianity, based in Constantinople and regarded as the mother church of most modern Eastern Orthodox churches.

napoleon.name: Napoleon
napoleon.summary: French emperor from 1804 to 1814, and briefly in 1815, who rose to power as a general during the French Revolution and led sweeping military campaigns across Europe and the Middle East.

cappadocian-greeks.name: Cappadocian Greeks
cappadocian-greeks.summary: An ethnic Greek community native to Cappadocia in Anatolia since antiquity, forced to resettle in Greece in 1923 under the Greek–Turkish population exchange.

richard-macgillivray-dawkins.name: Richard MacGillivray Dawkins
richard-macgillivray-dawkins.summary: British archaeologist and scholar of classical and modern Greek (1871–1955), who directed the British School at Athens from 1906 to 1913.

constitution-of-the-ottoman-empire.name: Ottoman Constitution
constitution-of-the-ottoman-empire.summary: The Ottoman Empire's first and only constitution, in effect 1876 to 1878 and 1908 to 1922, drafted by reformist Young Ottomans to check the sultan's autocratic rule.
